metadata.title: Gradient Descent, One Step at a Time
metadata.audience: makers and curious learners new to ML

beats.narration_text: Ciao, this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask: how does a neural network actually learn? Skip the hype. Show me the one rule underneath, with real numbers.

show.event: composer card fades in on cream
greeting 'Ciao, Liam' types above the composer
the ask types in
runningText 'working through the math…' appears
three result lines cascade in

props.segment: Gradient Descent, One Step at a Time
props.command: How does a neural network actually learn? Skip the hype. Show me the one rule underneath, with real numbers.
output: the rule: measure the slope of the error, step the other way
worked example: from 3 to 0.983 in five steps
where it breaks: the step size, and valleys that aren't the lowest

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask lands answered; Liam introduced in first breath.

beats.narration_text: Training a model keeps stepping downhill. It never searches for the best answer. It measures which way the error rises, takes a small step the other way, and repeats, step after step.

show.event: cream page holds; caret blinks
types 'Training a model / finds the best answer.'
'finds the best answer' turns terracotta, hesitates, backspaces
types 'keeps stepping downhill'
final lines settle: 'Training a model / keeps stepping downhill.'

props.text:
Training a model
finds the best answer.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — misconception corrected: training is not a search for the best answer; it is repeated local steps downhill.

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole picture. Across the bottom, one setting of the model. Call it theta. Up the side, the loss: how wrong the model is at that setting. The model sits somewhere on this curve, and it can't see the bottom. All it can measure is the slope right where it stands. The slope points uphill. So step the other way.

show.event: axes draw on; x labelled 'setting θ', y labelled 'loss'
the bowl L(θ)=θ² draws on
a terracotta ball lands at θ=3
tangent line draws through the ball: 'slope'
arrow points uphill, then a second arrow flips to point downhill: 'step'

shot.visual_intent: The loss curve as a landscape; the model only sees the local slope.
shot.motion_claim: The tangent at the ball IS the gradient; the downhill arrow is the step.

beats.narration_text: Written down, it's one line. The new setting becomes the old setting, minus a step. The step is two things multiplied: the slope of the loss right here, called the gradient, and eta, the step size, a number you choose. Steep slope, big step. Flat ground, tiny step. That minus sign is the whole idea: go against the slope.

show.event: update rule typesets: θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η ∇L(θ_t)
spotlight on θ_{t+1}; label below: 'new setting'
spotlight on θ_t; label: 'current setting'
spotlight on ∇L(θ_t); label: 'slope of the loss here'
spotlight on η; label: 'step size (you choose it)'
spotlight on the minus sign: 'against the slope'

shot.visual_intent: The update rule with a moving spotlight and a glossary label per symbol.
shot.motion_claim: The spotlight walks the equation in narration order; the minus sign is the final accent.

beats.narration_text: Real numbers. Loss is theta squared, so the slope is two theta. Start at three, step size zero point one. Slope six, step zero point six: we land at two point four. Slope four point eight: one point nine two. Each step shrinks theta by the same factor, zero point eight. Five steps in, the loss fell from nine to just under one.

show.event: bowl and ball at θ=3; table header t | θ | slope | loss
ball steps to 2.4; row t=1 lands
ball steps to 1.92; row t=2 lands
rows t=3..5 land with each step; '×0.8 per step' chip appears
loss column highlights 9 → 0.9664

shot.visual_intent: Ball stepping down the bowl in lockstep with a table of executed values (demo/evidence.json).
shot.motion_claim: Each row lands exactly when the ball lands; the shrinking steps are the factor 0.8.

beats.narration_text: The step size is where this bites. Same bowl, same start, three choices. At zero point zero one, ten steps later theta has barely moved: two point four five. At zero point one, it's down to zero point three two. At one point one, every step overshoots the bottom and lands further out; after ten steps, theta is past eighteen. Too big, and it doesn't slow down. It runs away.

show.event: three bowls side by side, labelled η=0.01, η=0.1, η=1.1
left ball creeps; counter settles at θ₁₀ = 2.4512
middle ball rolls in; counter θ₁₀ = 0.3221
right ball zig-zags across the bottom, each bounce wider; terracotta
right counter climbs to θ₁₀ = 18.5752

shot.visual_intent: Three learning rates on the same bowl, side by side, with θ after 10 executed steps.
shot.motion_claim: Crawl vs converge vs diverge happen simultaneously so the comparison is held, not narrated.

beats.narration_text: The second failure: the slope only knows where you are. This loss has two valleys. Start on the right, and the ball settles into the shallow one, at a loss of minus one point oh seven, and stops, because the slope there is zero. The deeper valley, at minus three point five one, is right next door, and gradient descent never sees it. Where you start decides where you end.

show.event: two-valley curve L(θ)=θ⁴−3θ²+θ draws on
ball drops at θ=2 and rolls into the right valley
label at rest: 'loss -1.0702', slope chip '0'
left valley lights terracotta: 'loss -3.5139'
ghost ball from θ=−2 rolls into the deep valley: start decides end

shot.visual_intent: A non-convex loss where gradient descent stops in the shallower valley (executed).
shot.motion_claim: The ball physically stops in the wrong valley while the deeper one is lit beside it.

beats.narration_text: Real models run a version of this same rule on millions, even billions, of settings at once, so the bowl becomes a landscape you can't draw. Two tricks make that affordable. Backpropagation computes every slope in one backward pass. And each step looks at a small batch: here, eight points out of two hundred. The path wobbles, but each step costs a twenty-fifth as much, and the fit lands within a few percent.

show.event: contour map of the loss over two settings (w, b) fades in
chip: 'backpropagation: every slope in one backward pass'
smooth ink path: 'all 200 points per step' draws to the minimum
wobbly terracotta path: '8 points per step' draws beside it
end chips: loss 0.15 vs 0.1533

shot.visual_intent: Full-batch vs mini-batch paths on a real 2-parameter fit (seeded, executed).
shot.motion_claim: The two paths draw simultaneously; the wobble is visible and both reach the valley.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Loss measures how wrong the model is, and the gradient is its slope. Each step, the new setting is the old setting minus the step size times the slope. The step size decides it: too small crawls, too big runs away. It finds a valley, not necessarily the lowest one. Where you start decides which valley you end in. And at scale: backpropagation for the slopes, small batches for speed.

show.event: verdict artifact card in on cream
heading types
lines 1–5 land on their spoken cue

artifactLines: Loss measures how wrong the model is; the gradient is its slope.
Each step: new setting = old setting − step size × slope.
The step size decides it: too small crawls, too big runs away.
It finds a valley, not necessarily the lowest one.
Where you start decides which valley you end in.
At scale: backpropagation for the slopes, small batches for speed.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a short Python script, no M L libraries, that runs gradient descent on loss equals theta squared, starting at theta equals three, for ten steps, with step sizes zero point zero one, zero point one, zero point nine and one point one. Print theta after every step. Then, using only the printed numbers, tell me which runs converge, which oscillate, which blow up, and predict the largest step size that still converges. Here's what to check. Zero point one should go three, two point four, one point nine two. Zero point nine is the interesting one: it flips sign every step and still lands. And watch whether Claude derives the cutoff from the numbers, or just asserts it. If it says one, ask it why.

props.command: Write a short Python script, no ML libraries, that runs gradient descent on loss = theta squared, starting at theta = 3, for 10 steps, with step sizes 0.01, 0.1, 0.9 and 1.1. output: check: the slope is 2 × theta, and 0.1 goes 3 → 2.4 → 1.92
check: 0.9 flips sign every step but still shrinks
check: the cutoff is derived from the numbers, not asserted
